verses.zh: 我们既蒙留下，有进入他安息的应许，就当畏惧，免得我们（原文是你们）中间或有人似乎是赶不上了。
verses.en: Therefore we must be wary[NOTE:1] that, while the promise of entering his rest remains open, none of you may seem to have come short of it.
verses.commentary:
4:1 "Therefore" Based on the truths of chapters 1-3.

▣

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"fear"

NRSV, TEV
"take care"

NJB
"Beware"

The VERB is an AORIST PASSIVE (deponent) SUBJUNCTIVE
("let us fear"). The warnings of Hebrews (cf. Heb. 2:1-4; 3:7-13; 4:1-13; 5:11-6:12; 10:26-39; and 12:14-17) should
elicit a sense of dread (cf. Heb. 4:11). These warnings touch ultimate issues of salvation and assurance.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NT EVIDENCE OF ONE'S SALVATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN ASSURANCE

▣ "while a promise remains of entering His rest" This is a continuing word play (i.e.,
"His rest," cf. Heb. 4:1,3,5,8,9,10,11) in which the author uses rabbinical hermeneutical methodology to
talk about the people of God's history and hope.

- Gen. 2:2, God's rest on the seventh day of creation

- Num. 13-14, Joshua's rest which was the Promised Land

- Ps. 95:7-11, God's rest was still available in David's day

- Heb. 4:1, 10-11, the day of rest as a reference to peace with God and life with God (heaven) is still available

▣

NASB, NKJV
"to have come short of it"

NRSV
"to have failed to reach it"

TEV
"to have failed to receive that promised rest"

NJB
"that he has come too later for the promise of entering his place of rest"

Peshitta
"find they are prevented from entering"

This reflects a Hebrew term chatha ("miss the mark") translated as hamartia
by the Septuagint, meaning "fall short" or "come short" (cf. Heb. 12:15; Rom. 3:23). A related meaning is
"come too late" (cf. NJB).

Remember, the writers of the NT were Hebrew thinkers writing in Koine Greek. Therefore,
word meaning must be drawn from the Septuagint (i.e., Koine Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible translated several
centuries before the NT), and not Greek poets, philosophers, historians (i.e., Greek lexicons). There is a lexicon and
concordance of the Septuagint available in English (Edwin Hatch, Henry Redpath, Concordance to the Septuagint,
published by Baker, ISBN 0-8010-4270-4).

verses.zh: 因为有福音传给我们，像传给他们一样；只是所听见的道与他们无益，因为他们没有信心与所听见的道调和。
verses.en: For we had good news proclaimed to us just as they did. But the message they heard did them no good, since they did not join in[NOTE:1] with those who heard it in faith.[NOTE:2]
notes: A few mss (א and a few versional witnesses) have the nominative singular participle συγκεκερασμένος (sunkekerasmenos, “since it [the message] was not combined with faith by those who heard it”), a reading that refers back to the ὁ λόγος (ho logos, “the message”). There are a few other variants here (e.g., συγκεκεραμμένοι [sunkekerammenoi] in 104, συγκεκεραμένους [sunkekeramenous] in 1881 M), but the accusative plural participle συγκεκερασμένους (sunkekerasmenous), found in P13vid,46 A B C D* Ψ 0243 0278 33 81 1739 2464, has by far the best external credentials. This participle agrees with the previous ἐκείνους (ekeinous, “those”), a more difficult construction grammatically than the nominative singular. Thus, both on external and internal grounds, συγκεκερασμένους is preferred.
verses.commentary:
4:2 "we have had good news preached to us" The "good news" refers to the gospel about Jesus Christ, who all
may accept by faith (cf. Eph. 2:8-9). Before Christ it referred to God's Word, which was given in the OT in different ways
(i.e., "do not eat of the tree"; "build an ark"; "follow Me to a land"; "keep the law"; "enter the Promised
Land," etc.). Each person or group had to believe God and respond by faith (i.e., act on) His Word to them.
In the Exodus the ones believing were Joshua and Caleb. They believed God's promise about the Promised Land;
most Israelis did not. They entered "the rest," but all the adults of that generation from 20 years old up, did not. They died
in the wilderness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA
OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "just as they also" This refers to the Israelites who listened to the ten spies' negative
report. Joshua and Caleb, however, did not doubt God's promise about conquering the Promised Land (cf.
Numbers 13-14), but had faith, so they could enter Canaan, but their unbelieving contemporaries could not.

▣

NASB
"because it was not united by faith in those who heard"

NKJV, Peshitta
"not being mixed with faith in those who heard it"

NRSV
"because they were not united by faith with those who listened"

TEV
"they did not accept it with faith"

NJB
"because they did not share the faith of those who did listen"

There is a Greek manuscript variation in this phrase. The best attested reading has a
PERFECT PASSIVE ACCUSATIVE MASCULINE PLURAL PARTICIPLE, which would refer to the faith
of Joshua and Caleb (cf. NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB). The other option is a PERFECT PASSIVE NOMINATIVE
MASCULINE SINGULAR PARTICIPLE, which would refer to faith in the message heard (cf. TEV, NJB, NIV).

The theological issue involves the faith (salvation) or lack of faith of the Israelite
adults (20 years and up) who participated in the exodus. Did their lack of faith in the spies' report mean
that

- they were not allowed to enter Canaan

- they were not allowed to enter heaven?

This question is not easy to answer because of the author's word play on the term "rest." It seems
best to affirm their initial faith in YHWH (i.e., salvation), but admit they lacked the faith to trust His
every promise (i.e., taking Canaan). This is the very question related to the first century readers. Was
their lack of persistence a sign they were never saved or did it show their weak faith? In his commentary
on Hebrews in The New International Commentary Series, F. F. Bruce says,

The practical implication is clear: it is not the hearing of the gospel by itself that
brings salvation, but its appropriation by faith; and if a genuine faith, it will be a persistent
faith" (p. 73).

verses.zh: 但我们已经相信的人得以进入那安息，正如　神所说：「我在怒中起誓说：『他们断不可进入我的安息！』」其实造物之工，从创世以来已经成全了。
verses.en: For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my anger, ‘They will never enter my rest!’”[NOTE:1] And yet God’s works[NOTE:2] were accomplished from the foundation of the world.
notes: Grk “although the works,” continuing the previous reference to God. The referent (God) is specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
4:3 "just as He said" This is a PERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE, which is repeatedly used
to refer to inspired Scripture (cf. Heb. 1:13; 4:3,4; 10:5,9; 13:5). The PRONOUN "He" can refer to
God the Father or God the Son.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE
(ITS UNIQUENESS AND INSPIRATION)

▣ This is a quote from Ps. 95:11 (as are Heb. 4:5 and 3:11), but also an added OT allusion back
to Gen. 2:2, God's Sabbath (the seventh-day rest of creation).

▣ "from the foundation of the world" God had a plan for creation both before and after the Fall of Genesis 3.
God is in control of time and space. He is both Creator and Redeemeer.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOUNDATIONS OF THE EARTH (both "from" or "before")

verses.zh: 论到第七日，有一处说：「到第七日，　神就歇了他一切的工。」
verses.en: For he has spoken somewhere about the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,”[NOTE:1]
verses.commentary:
4:4 "For He has said somewhere" This reflects a rabbinical idiom of belief in the inspiration of the
entire OT (cf. Heb. 2:6). The "where" (i.e., the exact location of the text) and "who" (i.e., the human
author or editor of the text), were not as important as God's authorship of all Scripture (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:20-21). This does
not imply the author forgot where the OT reference was to be found.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "seventh day" The rabbis asserted that God's Sabbath (i.e., "the Day
of Rest") never ceased because the regular formula of Genesis 1, "there was evening and there was morning,
day. . .," is never mentioned in connection with this seventh day of creation in Gen. 2:2,3 (cf. Exod. 20:11). This is
a rabbinical type interpretation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SABBATH (OT)

verses.zh: 又有一处说：「他们断不可进入我的安息！」
verses.en: but to repeat the text cited earlier:[NOTE:1] “They will never enter my rest!”
verses.commentary: 4:5 This is a quote from Psalm 95:11.

verses.zh: 既有必进安息的人，那先前听见福音的，因为不信从，不得进去。
verses.en: Therefore it remains for some to enter it, yet those to whom it was previously proclaimed did not enter because of disobedience.
verses.commentary:
4:6 "because of disobedience" Faithlessness is evidenced by disobedience (cf. Heb. 3:18; 4:6,11). The
larger context of chapter 4 reflects the events recorded in Numbers 13-14, but the specific scriptural
reference is Ps. 95:7-11, which relates to Israel's experience at Meribah.

The term "disobedience" (UBS4, NRSV, NKJV, NET) is in the ancient Greek uncial manuscripts
A, B, D, while "unbelief" is in the papyri manuscript P46, and the ancient uncial manuscript
א (REB, NJB, TEV). The NOUN "disobedience" is repeated in v. 11.

verses.zh: 所以过了多年，就在大卫的书上，又限定一日，如以上所引的说：「你们今日若听他的话，就不可硬着心。」
verses.en: So God[NOTE:1] again ordains a certain day, “Today,” speaking through David[NOTE:2] after so long a time, as in the words quoted before,[NOTE:3] “Oh, that today you would listen as he speaks![NOTE:4] Do not harden your hearts.”
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Ps 95 in the Hebrew does not mention David either in the text or the superscription. The writer of Hebrews might attribute Psalms as a whole to David, though some psalms are specifically attributed to other individuals or groups. Yet the Greek inscription for Ps 95 in the LXX credits the psalm to David, and the author of Hebrews frequently uses the LXX.
Grk “as it has been said before” (see Heb 3:7).
Grk “today if you hear his voice.”
verses.commentary:
4:7 "fixes a certain day, "Today," saying through David" The Greek term "fixes" is the English term
"horizon," which means a setting of bounds. "Through David" is not in the Hebrew text of Ps. 95:7-8, but
the Septuagint correctly interprets and inserts the traditional author of the Psalm. The author's argument
is based on God's rest still being open even during David's reign.

Psalm 95:7-11 has been quoted several times in the context of chapters 3 and 4. Each time a
different part of the OT passage is emphasized (like a sermon).

- Heb. 3:7-11 emphasizes "do not harden your hearts" of Ps. 95:8

- Heb. 3:15 emphasizes "when they provoked Me" of Ps. 95:9

- Heb. 4:3,5 emphasizes "they shall not enter My rest" of Ps. 95:11

- Heb. 4:7 emphasizes "today" of Ps. 95:7

See my full exegetical notes on Psalm 95 online at www.freebiblecommentary.org

verses.zh: 若是约书亚已叫他们享了安息，后来　神就不再提别的日子了。
verses.en: For if Joshua had given them rest, God[NOTE:1] would not have spoken afterward about another day.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
4:8 "if" This is a SECOND CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which is often called "contrary
to fact." Joshua did not bring all of the children of Israel into rest. This is using the term "rest" not
in the sense of Canaan, but God's spiritual rest (cf. Heb. 4:9-10). From Heb. 4:8-10 it is obvious that the
author of Hebrews is using "rest" in several historical/theological senses:

- the Promised Land of Canaan (Heb. 4:8, Joshua's day, Num. 13-14)

- the opportunity to trust God (cf. Heb. 4:9 i.e., David's day, Ps. 95)

- the Genesis 2 (Heb. 4:4) rest of God at creation (Heb. 4:10)

- heaven (Heb. 4:1 and 11)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII

▣ "hearts" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "Joshua" The King James translation has "Jesus," which follows the Geneva and Bishops Bibles'
translations, but the context demands the OT "Joshua" (Peshitta). Both names are spelled the same (i.e.,
Joshua ‒ Hebrew; Jesus ‒ Aramaic)! They are a combination of two NOUNS (YHWH and salvation)
to which one must supply a VERB. The early church often used Joshua as a type of Jesus
(cf. Acts 7:45, where the same error in translation is made).

▣ "He" This must refer to the Divine author of Psalm 95.

verses.zh: 这样看来，必另有一安息日的安息为　神的子民存留。
verses.en: Consequently a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.
verses.commentary:
4:9 This is the summary of the author's exposition of Psalm 95. There was

- an initial promise of rest (cf. Gen. 2:2)

- a historical fulfillment (Joshua)

- a later opportunity (David's day)

- still a fourth opportunity for anyone who chooses to exercise faith in God's promises

Notice the author is using the title "the people of God" for those who believe in
Christ (not just Jews).

verses.zh: 因为那进入安息的，乃是歇了自己的工，正如　神歇了他的工一样。
verses.en: For the one who enters God’s[NOTE:1] rest has also rested from his works, just as God did from his own works.
notes: Grk “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
4:10,11 All of the VERBALS of Heb. 4:10-11 are AORIST, which either

- point to a completed action

- view all of life as a whole

Verses 10 and 11 make it clear that the "rest" of Heb. 4:10 refers to heaven. Believers will one
day cease their diligence (cf. Rev. 14:13), but Heb. 4:11 clearly asserts that while physical life remains,
believers must continue in faith, repentance, obedience, and perseverance. Verse 11 is a strong warning.
Salvation is absolutely free in the finished work of Christ. It is a gift of grace from the Father and the
convicting work of the Spirit. However, the sovereign Triune God has chosen to deal with humanity in a
covenant relationship. Mankind must respond and continue to respond. Salvation is not a ticket to heaven
nor a fire insurance policy, but a day-by-day faith relationship with God which issues in progressive
Christlikeness! The covenant has benefits and obligations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

verses.zh: 所以，我们务必竭力进入那安息，免得有人学那不信从的样子跌倒了。
verses.en: Thus we must make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by following the same pattern of disobedience.
verses.commentary:
4:11

NASB, NKJV
"Let us be diligent to enter that rest"

NRSV
"Let us make every effort to enter that rest"

TEV
"Let us do our best to receive that rest"

NJB
"Let us press forward to enter this place of rest"

Peshitta
"Let us strive therefore to enter into that rest"

In English this seems to advocate human performance in attaining God's rest, but the Greek
word means "to be eager," "to make haste" (cf. 2 Thess. 2:17; 2 Tim. 4:9).

▣ "so that no one will fall through following the same example of disobedience" See full
note at Heb. 3:18 and 4:6.

verses.zh: 神的道是活泼的，是有功效的，比一切两刃的剑更快，甚至魂与灵，骨节与骨髓，都能刺入、剖开，连心中的思念和主意都能辨明。
verses.en: For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any double-edged sword, piercing even to the point of dividing soul from spirit, and joints from marrow; it is able to judge the desires and thoughts of the heart.
verses.commentary:
4:12 "word of God" Verses 12 and 13 form one sentence in Greek. The term word (logos) does not
refer personally to Jesus, as it does in John 1:1, but to God's spoken (cf. Heb. 13:7) or written message
either through the OT Scriptures or NT revelation. God's self-revelation is described in three ways:

- it is personified as having a life of its own

- it is like the penetrating power of a sword

- it is like an all-knowing judge (cf. Heb. 4:13)

In his book Jewish Christianity, H. E. Dana makes the suggestion based on Egyptian papyri
usage that "word" (logos) means "reckoning" or "calling into account." He asserts this fits the original
author's overall argument, that there will be a divine reckoning through examination, using the image
of a surgeon (p. 227). Therefore, this text is not a description of the revealed word of God, but the
discerning judgment of God. This is interesting, but the author of Hebrews used logos often for God's
word (cf. Heb. 2:2; 4:2; 5:13; 7:28; 13:7) and also the Greek term for the spoken word, rhēma
(cf. Heb. 6:5; 11:3).

The best way to define Greek words used in the NT period by Jewish people is a lexicon to the
Septuagint. This Koine Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible was by rabbis in the second century before Jesus. It
differs some from the MT, but copies of both were found in the Dead Sea Scrolls. See James Moulton and George
Milligan, The Vocabulary of the Greek Testament: Illustrated from the Papyri and Other None Literary Sources.

▣ "living and active and sharper" This reflects the Hebrew concept of the power of the spoken
word of God (cf. Gen 1:1,3,6,9,14,20,24,26; Ps. 33:6,9; 148:5; Isa. 40:8; 45:23; 55:11,17-19; Matt. 5:17-19;
24:35; 1 Pet. 1:23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOGOS (word)

▣ "sharper than any two-edged sword" This speaks of the penetrating power of God's word
(cf. John 12:48 and Rev. 1:6; 2:12,16, where it is used of Jesus).

▣ "soul and spirit" This is not an affirmation of an ontological dichotomy in mankind, but a dual relationship
to both this planet and to God. The Hebrew word nephesh is used of both mankind and the animals in
Genesis, while "spirit" (ruah) is used uniquely of mankind. God's word penetrates mankind's inner
self. This is not a proof-text on the nature of mankind as a two-part (dichotomous)
or three-part (trichotomous) being (cf. 1 Thess 5:23). Mankind is primarily represented in the Bible as a
unity (cf. Gen. 2:7).

For a good summary of the theories of mankind as trichotomous, dichotomous, or a unity,
see Millard J. Erickson's Christian Theology (second edition) pp. 538-557 and Frank Stagg's
Polarities of Man's Existence in Biblical Perspective.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

SPECIAL TOPIC: BODY AND SPIRIT

▣ "and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart" In Hebrew thought the "heart"
represents the entire person and their inner motivation. God knows true faith and fake faith.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

verses.zh: 并且被造的没有一样在他面前不显然的；原来万物在那与我们有关系的主眼前，都是赤露敞开的。
verses.en: And no creature is hidden from God,[NOTE:1] but everything is naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must render an account.
notes: Grk “him”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
4:13 "but all things are open and laid bare" God knows us completely (cf. 1 Sam. 16:7; Ps. 7:9;
33:13-15; 139:1-4; Prov. 16:2; 21:2; 24:12; Jer. 11:20; 17:10; 20:12; Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24; 15:8;
Rom. 8:27). Humans' lives and thoughts are an open book to their Creator.

▣

NASB
"open and laid bare"

NKJV, Peshitta
"naked and open"

NRSV
"naked and laid bare"

TEV
"exposed and lies open"

NJB
"uncovered and stretched fully open"

This imagery literally means "to expose the neck by lifting the chin." This OT imagery
was a warning to judges; here it refers to meeting God face-to-face on judgment day, who has full knowledge
of our motives (see note above).

verses.zh: 我们既然有一位已经升入高天尊荣的大祭司，就是　神的儿子耶稣，便当持定所承认的道。
verses.en: Therefore since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession.
verses.commentary:
4:14 "a great high priest" The author first mentions Jesus as High Priest in Heb. 3:1-6. After the
warnings and exhortations of Heb. 3:7-4:13, he now returns to the topic. Hebrews 1:14-7:28 uses Psalm 110 as a key text. This same
pattern is followed in the warnings in Heb. 5:11-6:12 and in the discussion of Jesus' priestly functions in Heb. 6:13-10:39.

Hebrews is the only book in the NT that calls Jesus the High Priest." The author's comparison
of the Mosaic covenant and the new covenant continues. This would have been hard for the Jewish people to
accept and understand. Jesus was not of the priestly tribe of Levi. However, Jesus is called "a priest" in
Heb. 1:3; 2:17,18; 3:1. In the OT the Messiah is referred to as priest in only two contexts: Psalm 110 and
Zechariah 4, both of which have both royal and priestly aspects.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS AS HIGH PRIEST

▣ "who has passed through the heavens" This is in the PERFECT TENSE. Jesus has
passed through the heavens (whether there are 3 or 7), He returned to the Father's presence (i.e., Acts 1), and the result
of His coming (incarnation) and going (ascension, cf. Luke 24:50-51; John 3:13; 6:62; 14:2; 16:5,10,28; 20:17; Acts 1:6-11;
Eph. 1:20; 4:8-10; 1 Tim. 3:16; Heb. 1:3; 4:14; 9:24) remains. Therefore, believers can now, through His agency,
also pass through the heavens. In Gnostic thought, the heavens are angelic barriers (aeons), but in the OT
they are

- the atmosphere where birds fly

- the windows of heaven where rain comes from

- the starry heavens of the sun and moon

- the very presence of God

There has been much discussion by the rabbis as to whether there are three or seven heavens
(cf. Eph. 4:10; 2 Cor. 12:2). This phrase was also used by the rabbis to describe the heavenly tabernacle,
which fits this context best (cf. Heb. 9:23-28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GNOSTICISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

▣ "Jesus" It is possible that this is a typological play on Jesus as the new Joshua. Their names
are exactly the same (i.e., Joshua ‒ Hebrew; Jesus ‒ Aramaic). The author of Hebrews alludes to
the Exodus material extensively. As Joshua brought God's people into the rest of the Promised Land, so too,
will Jesus bring them into heaven.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRIST JESUS AS LORD, #2

▣ "the Son of God" This is both an OT divine title applied to Jesus of Nazareth and also the
author's continuing emphasis on Jesus as "son" (cf. Heb. 1:2; 3:6; 5:8; 7:28). It is not by accident that
the humanity and Deity of Jesus are emphasized together by the title "Son of Man" (cf. Ezek. 2:1 -
human; Dan. 7:13 - divine). This is the main NT truth about the person of Christ (cf. John 1:1,14; 1 John 4:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "let us hold fast our confession" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE. This is the
continuing emphasis on the need for perseverance (cf. Heb. 2:1; 3:6,14). Believers must balance their initial decision
(cf. John 1:12; 3:16; Rom. 10:9-13) with ongoing discipleship (cf. Matt. 7:13-27; 13:18-23; 28:19-20; Eph. 1:4;
2:10). Both are crucial! Faith must issue in faithfulness! For a discussion of the term "confession," see note
at Heb. 3:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONFESSION/PROFESSION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NEED TO PERSEVERE

verses.zh: 因我们的大祭司并非不能体恤我们的软弱。他也曾凡事受过试探，与我们一样，只是他没有犯罪。
verses.en: For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin.
verses.commentary:
4:15 "sympathize with our weakness" A. T. Robertson gives another possible alternative translation,
"suffer with our weakness" (cf. Heb. 2:17-18). Jesus never had a sin nature and never yielded to sin, but
He was exposed to true temptation because of mankind's sin.

▣ "tempted" The term (peirazō) has the connotation of "to tempt with a view toward
destruction" (cf. Heb. 2:18; 3:9; 11:37). It is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, which emphasizes
a finished state by means of an outside agent, such as the tempter. This term is a title for Satan ("the one
tempting") in Matt. 4:3 (also notice Mark 1:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK TERMS FOR TESTING AND THEIR CONNOTATIONS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONAL EVIL

▣ "in all things as we are yet without sin" Jesus is both fully God and fully human, and
yet He understands us! However, He does not participate in fallen mankind's rebellion and independence from
the Father (i.e., the innocent, sinless One, cf. Heb. 2:17-18; 7:26; Luke 23:41; John 8:46; 14:30;
2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 2:7-8; 1 Pet. 1:19; 2:22; 3:18; 1 John 3:5).

verses.zh: 所以，我们只管坦然无惧地来到施恩的宝座前，为要得怜恤，蒙恩惠，作随时的帮助。
verses.en: Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.[NOTE:1]
verses.commentary:
4:16 "Therefore let us draw near" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) SUBJUNCTIVE,
which emphasizes the subject's continual involvement, but with an element of contingency. This is a technical
term in the Septuagint (LXX) for a priest approaching God. In Hebrews this term is used of fallen mankind's
ability to approach God because of Jesus' sacrifice (cf. Heb. 4:16; 7:25; 10:1,22; 11:6). Jesus has made His
followers a "kingdom of priests" (i.e., an OT title for Israel, cf. Exod.19:5,6; 1 Pet. 2:5,9; Rev. 1:6).

▣ "with confidence to the throne of grace" The term "confidence" means "freedom to boldly speak."
We have freedom, and therefore, boldness, to approach the very presence of God through Jesus Christ
(cf. Heb. 10:19,35). This is similar to the symbol of the torn veil of Herod's temple in Jerusalem on the
day that Jesus died (i.e., from top to bottom, cf. Matt. 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45). Through Jesus, sinful people can come
before a holy God where they receive mercy and grace, not condemnation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOLDNESS

▣ "to the throne of grace" This may be a circumlocution for God, like the use of the
PASSIVE VOICE. The author of Hebrews views heaven as a spiritual tabernacle
(cf. Heb. 9:11,24), but also a heavenly throne (cf. Heb. 1:8; 4:16; 8:1; 12:2).

▣ "to help in time of need" The context speaks of warnings against not holding fast our
confession. God will surely help us in times of trials and temptations

- through Jesus

- by His own character

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- The author moves back and forth between the superiority of Jesus and warning to hold fast to Him.

- Jesus' superiority (new covenant) over Moses (old covenant)

- He is the superior revelation (from the prophets, Heb. 1:1-3)

- He is the superior mediator (from angels, Heb. 1:4-2:18)

- He is the superior servant (from Moses, Heb. 3:1-6)

- He is the superior priest (from Aaron, Heb. 4:14-5:10; 6:13-7:28)

- He is the superior covenant (from the OT, Heb. 8:1-13; 9:15-22)

- He is the superior sanctuary (from the temple, Heb. 9:1-11, 23-28)

- He is the superior sacrifice (from animals, Heb. 9:12-14; 10:1-18)

- He is the superior mountain (from the old covenant as Mt. Sinai and new covenant as Mt. Zion,
Heb. 12:18-29)

- In light of Jesus' superiority there is a series of warnings against

- rejecting His gospel (i.e., the New Covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36)

- reverting to Judaism (i.e., Old Covenant)

- Heb. 2:1-4

- Heb. 3:7-4:13

- Heb. 5:11-6:12

- Heb. 10:19-39

- Heb. 12:14-29
